# Research notes on 2 Timothy 2, verse by verse

I couldn't cover every verse equally. The fullest sources I could read were Guzik's Enduring Word commentary, several Precept Austin pages, and short StudyLight excerpts (Henry, Gill, Wesley, Barnes, Calvin, Ellicott, Clarke, Barclay). I couldn't open the Gill, Ellicott or Pulpit verse pages on BibleHub, so some verses have thin notes. The gaps are listed at the end.

---

## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- Guzik says Paul gives Timothy a specific way to be strong: by grace. "Grace" here means "the divine help, the unmerited gift of assistance that comes from God" (he is quoting White). He adds that God's strength doesn't come while we sit back passively, but as we seek and rely on Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Precept Austin points out that "be strong" is in the passive voice. Paul is not telling Timothy to be strong in his own strength. It means being "made strong," which is supernatural rather than natural strength. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_21-7

**v. 2:**
- Guzik: Timothy was to pass on simple apostolic teaching and example, not his own ideas, pouring into others what Paul had poured into him. The quality to look for is faithfulness, not cleverness, popularity or looks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Clarke and Barnes both think "many witnesses" may point to Timothy's ordination. Clarke links it to the time when Paul laid his hands on him before many witnesses (1 Tim 6:12). Barnes suggests a solemn charge given before the church when Timothy was ordained. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/2-2.html
- Constable: just as Paul passed the torch to Timothy, Timothy should pass it to faithful men, who would in turn teach those after them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/2-2.html
- How this verse bears on apostolic succession is disputed; see Parts 2 and 3.

**vv. 3–4:**
- Guzik: Timothy must have the attitude of a soldier who expects hardship, and no good soldier quits just because hardship comes. The things that entangle a soldier may be good or bad in themselves; the soldier must give up whatever makes him less effective. Guzik cites Clarke, who notes (from Grotius) that Roman legionaries were barred from farming and trade. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Precept Austin: the Greek word for "entangle" means being caught up in something that hinders and obstructs. It adds a caution: family, social and business duties still have to be done, and the emphasis falls on the word "entangleth". https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_23-4
- Matthew Henry: all Christians, and ministers especially, are soldiers of Jesus Christ who fight under his banner. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm

**v. 5:**
- Guzik: an athlete can't make up the rules. He applies it to people who say "God understands" while carrying on in a known sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/

**v. 6:**
- Guzik: the farmer stands for unglamorous, hard work, balanced by Paul's own words that his labour was really God's grace at work in him (1 Cor 15:10). "First to partake" means the pastor must feed on the Word himself before he can feed others. The harvest comes at the end of the age, not at the end of the meeting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Precept Austin sums up vv. 3–6: endure like a soldier, strive like an athlete, toil patiently like a farmer. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_23-4

**v. 7:**
- Matthew Henry: unless the One who gave the revelation also gives understanding in the heart, we are nothing. So we pray for understanding but also urge people to think things over, because considering is the way to understand. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm
- Guzik reads vv. 3–7 as one lesson about perseverance: the soldier, athlete and farmer who stop too soon never see the victory, the prize or the harvest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/

**v. 8:**
- Guzik: "seed of David" shows Jesus was the Messiah of Israel. The cross was the payment and the resurrection the receipt. He also says "seed of David" shows Jesus was fully man and "raised from the dead" shows He was fully God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Barclay: the Greek tense describes a lasting state rather than a single past event, so the sense is "remember your risen and ever-present Lord". https://studylight.org/commentaries/dsb/2-timothy-2.html

**v. 9:**
- Matthew Henry: persecutors can silence preachers, but they can't stop the Word working on hearts and consciences. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm
- Guzik: Scripture stands for ever, but it can be "bound" when pastors abandon it or treat it as decoration. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/

**v. 10:**
- Paul Jeon (TGC) sees an apparent paradox: belief in God's sovereignty might lead to passivity. Instead, Paul keeps going precisely because God has chosen some for salvation. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/2-timothy/
- Ironside: though imprisoned as a criminal, Paul had a clear conscience because he was there for the gospel's sake. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/2-timothy-2.html

**v. 11:**
- Wesley reads "dead with him" as dead to sin, and ready to die for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_timothy/2.htm
- Precept Austin reports that the Bible Knowledge Commentary firmly links "if we died with Him" to baptism as explained in Romans 6. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_212-14

**v. 12:**
- Guzik: the saying promises faithful believers an eternal reward, and that reward is worth more than anything gained by quitting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- MacArthur (via Precept Austin): "deny" is in the future tense ("if we ever deny Him"), pointing to a moment when confessing Christ costs a great deal and so tests whether faith is real. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_212-14
- Interpreters differ on this verse; see Part 2.

**v. 13:**
- Guzik: no amount of human faithlessness disproves God's faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Alford, persuaded by Ellicott, says the Greek word behind "faithless" always seems to mean "unbelief" in the New Testament, not "unfaithfulness". https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_212-14
- This is the most debated verse in the chapter; see Part 2.

**v. 14:**
- Matthew Henry: the minister's work is not to tell people what they never knew, but to remind them of what they already know. He adds that people who love to argue usually argue about small things, and battles over words do great harm. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm

**v. 15:**
- Guzik: "rightly dividing" means knowing what Scripture says and doesn't say, and how it is and isn't to be understood. Sprinkling a few verses into sermons as illustrations isn't enough. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Matthew Henry: handling the word of truth rightly takes great wisdom, study and care. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm
- Precept Austin warns that getting too heated or dogmatic over unclear terms makes us the very word-quarrellers Paul criticises. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_215-19

**vv. 16–17:**
- Precept Austin: Paul isn't talking about gossip here. He means destructive heresy that twists divine truth. The present-tense command makes avoiding such talk a way of life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_216-17
- Matthew Henry: error runs downhill; grant one absurdity and a thousand follow. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm

**v. 18:**
- Matthew Henry: Hymenaeus and Philetus didn't openly deny the resurrection. They reinterpreted it as purely spiritual or allegorical, and so already past. Anything that removes the future life overthrows Christian faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm
- Guzik applies the "faith of some" to the excuse "I eat the meat and spit out the bones": some people will choke on the bones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) compares this error to the Jehovah's Witness teaching that Jesus returned invisibly in 1914. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/2-2.html

**v. 19:**
- Guzik: whatever the attacks, God's kingdom cannot be shaken. He reads the two "seals" as showing that election and sanctification belong together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/

**v. 20:**
- Precept Austin sets out more than one view. One says the visible church will always contain both consistent believers (gold and silver) and others who fall short (wood and clay). The writer prefers another: the contrast is between believers and unbelievers, both of whom can be found in the large house. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_220-26
- Arend Remmers (StudyLight book overview) sees the "great house" as a sign of decline: Paul could no longer simply speak of "the house of God," because the departure had gone so far. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/por/tew/2-timothy.html

**v. 21:**
- Guzik: Christians shouldn't think of themselves as a super-spiritual class, yet some are more usable to God because they have cleansed themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Precept Austin: "cleanses" means "to clean thoroughly." Timothy is to separate from the vessels of dishonour in v. 20. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_220-26

**v. 22:**
- Guzik: you can't really say "yes" to God until you can say "no" to some other things. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Precept Austin: besides separating from bad men and bad doctrine, Timothy must separate from the desires of the flesh. It also quotes the Preacher's Commentary's definitions of righteousness, faith and love. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_222-23

**v. 23:**
- Precept Austin: Paul isn't forbidding responsible discussion of Scripture and theology. He forbids fruitless speculation that produces quarrels. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_222-23

**v. 24:**
- Guzik: a pastor's job is not to pick fights or look for conflict. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Precept Austin quotes a writer who says the Lord's servant should not fight just to win, even when defending truth, but with a kind spirit so that the bond of peace may be kept. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_224-26

**v. 25:**
- Ellicott: the Greek suggests the sense "if perchance at any time God might grant." It expresses a hope that at some point God's grace would change these opponents. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/2-25.html
- Clarke: bad as they were, they were not beyond the reach of God's mercy. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brv/2-timothy/2-25.html
- Interpreters differ on how God's gift and human response fit together; see Part 2.

**v. 26:**
- Precept Austin: the "snare" shows that those who resist the gospel are still caught in the devil's trap, deluded by him into doing his will. It also sets out the dispute over who "his will" refers to. One option is that they are taken captive by God's servant to do God's will; another is that they escape the devil's snare to do God's will. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_224-26

---

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 2: What exactly is passed on?**
- Guzik: this verse shows the real apostolic succession, a chain of faithful men handing on the apostles' teaching. He quotes Clarke calling claims to an unbroken line "stupid … idle and futile." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-2/
- Vine (via Precept Austin): there is no hint of apostolic succession here; Paul is arranging for the faith to be kept and handed on. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_21-7
- GTY (Grace to You, a Baptist site in your list) says the verse simply describes discipleship. It contains no suggestion of an infallible tradition equal to God's Word. https://www.gty.org/articles/A246/scripture-tradition-and-rome-part-3
- Some older commentators take a middle position, seeing ordination in the verse:
  - Barnes: "the reference is undoubtedly to ordination", but the true succession is found in good men qualified to teach, not merely in those who have been ordained.
  - Matthew Henry: Timothy must also ordain them, because no one should push himself into the ministry; it must be entrusted by those already in office.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/2-2.html
- For the Catholic view, see Part 3.

**vv. 12–13: Can a believer fall away? What does "He remains faithful" promise?**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** "if we deny him" is a warning meant to shake off laziness. Those who stop confessing Christ for fear of persecution have no part with Christ. https://www.studylight.org/bible/tgl/ceb/2-timothy/2-12.html
- **Gill:** he distinguishes kinds of denial. A total apostasy is one from which there is no recovery; Christ will disown such people. The excerpt also mentions denial where faith and love were not lost, as in Peter's case. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/2-timothy/2-12.html
- **Wesley (labelled Arminian by StudyLight):**
  - On v. 12, denying Him means doing so to escape suffering for him.
  - On v. 13: even if some don't believe, God will keep all his promises to those who do; his word cannot fail.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/2-timothy-2.html
- **Barnes:** v. 13 can't mean Christ will save people who live in sin, because v. 12 has just said the opposite. Christ stays true to his word, including his warnings. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/2-timothy/2-13.html
- **Matthew Henry** agrees that Christ is faithful to his threats as well as his promises. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ti/2Ti_002.cfm
- **Hiebert:** the second pair of lines warns that denial and unfaithfulness really do separate people from Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_212-14
- **John Stott** notes that "He remains faithful" is often taken as comfort that Christ won't turn from us even if we turn from him. The excerpt I could see doesn't give his own conclusion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_212-14
- **Coffman (labelled Arminian/Restoration Movement by StudyLight):** Peter denied Christ and was forgiven, but this verse means a final, deliberate repudiation, and v. 13 doesn't soften it. https://www.studylight.org/bible/tgl/ceb/2-timothy/2-12.html
- **Barclay** takes a gentler line: Christ stays true to anyone who, however often he has failed, has tried to be true to him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dsb/2-timothy-2.html

**v. 25: Is repentance God's gift alone?**
- **Gill:** repentance comes from God's effective grace, not from human power or the means used. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv2-timothy/2-25.html
- **Desiring God** (a Baptist, Calvinist-leaning site in your list) argues from "may perhaps" that God's desire for all to be saved doesn't lead him to save all. Because only God can overcome spiritual deadness, "God may grant repentance" is our only hope. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god-desires-all-to-be-saved-and-grants-repentance-to-some
- **Wesley** also calls it "wholly his work". So on this verse Wesley and Gill sound alike; the Arminian/Calvinist difference doesn't show up in these short notes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/2-25.html
- **Matthew Henry** adds a balance: the gift comes with a "peradventure," so we shouldn't despair of God's grace, but we shouldn't presume on it either. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/2-25.html
- **Barnes** reads the grammar differently, as "lest": the opponents set themselves against the truth so that they won't be brought to repentance. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/2-timothy/2-25.html

**v. 10: Election.** TGC's sovereignty reading is in Part 1. I didn't find an Arminian treatment of this verse.

---

## Part 3: Other views

**Catholic (v. 2):**
- Catholic Answers: Paul refers to four generations of apostolic succession. In its dialogue with an objector it argues for "both/and": the teaching was entrusted to faithful men, and both the teaching and the men matter. It links this to Titus 1:5 on ordaining presbyters and bishops. https://www.catholic.com/tract/apostolic-tradition and https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/does-christs-church-have-apostolic-succession
- The same Catholic Answers piece notes that the Orthodox, and some Episcopalians and Lutherans, also hold to apostolic succession. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/does-christs-church-have-apostolic-succession
- The Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent) quotes 2 Tim 2:2 as showing that the apostles understood their mission to need an unbroken lawful succession. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01648b.htm
- An evangelical reply from GotQuestions: apostolic succession is "read into" 2 Timothy 2:2 and similar verses. https://www.gotquestions.org/pope-papacy.html

**Context in the letter (TGC):** Jeon frames the chapter around one question: what to do when the false teachers seem to be winning. Paul's answer is to endure by remembering those who came before, and ultimately the gospel itself. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/2-timothy/

---

## What I couldn't find
- Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary on most verses. I only saw short excerpts on vv. 2, 12, 13 and 25.
- Any Orthodox reading (oca.org), or Chrysostom's homilies on this chapter (I saw them listed on Precept Austin but couldn't open them).
- NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey material.
- Teaching from Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican sources on this chapter.
- Material on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace uses of vv. 12–13 or v. 21.

These would need another round of searching.
